summary:
AstroPyre Intelligence is an interactive web dashboard built for NASA's Flame in Freefall: A SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data challenge. It turns NASA PSI combustion research into practical fire safety guidance that non-specialists can explore.
A shared context bar (Environment, Atmosphere, Gravity) links three modes: Materials & Flame (13-material catalog, flammability lab, flame and suppression canvas, investigation explorer, PSI evidence), Emergency (flame, CO/smoke and burn scenarios with response checklists) and Space & Earth Safety (product and polymer evaluation, Earth applications of space research). Environments range from the ISS and Moon or Mars habitats to an Earth lab.
AI is used transparently. Claude drafted sourced plain-language briefings, and an "Ask the sources" box calls a live model only inside claude.ai; everywhere else, AI Search runs locally over curated data. Every statement carries its source, verified evidence is separated from heuristic estimates, and the team is verifying the content.

It is a single client-side page (HTML5, CSS, Vanilla JavaScript, Canvas) on GitHub Pages with no backend, supporting safer material selection, emergency preparedness, Mars habitat readiness and safer products on Earth.
details:
AstroPyre Intelligence is an interactive web-based platform developed to bridge the gap between NASA's microgravity combustion research and practical fire safety applications. Drawing on NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) investigations such as BASS-II, FLEX, and ACME, the Saffire experiments, and lessons from historical incidents such as the 1997 Mir fire, our project transforms complex scientific information into accessible, interactive insights that support fire safety awareness and informed decision-making.

Built around a shared top context bar that synchronizes Environment (Space Station/ISS, Lunar Surface Base, Mars Habitat, Earth Lab/Industrial Facility, or Custom), Atmosphere (oxygen and pressure), and Gravity (0 g, Moon, Mars, 1 g), the platform is organized into three complementary modes:

Materials & Flame: Allows users to select from 13 materials (including PMMA, Nomex III, Nomex HT90-40, Ultem 1000, Kapton, PTFE, Cotton, Wool, Nylon, Silicone, Polyethylene, Polypropylene, and polyurethane foam), read a flammability index, and visualize flame and suppression behavior on an interactive HTML5 Canvas. Sub-sections add an Investigation Explorer, Evidence from PSI, AI Insights, and Earth Applications (fine water mist extinguishers, smoke detection, firefighter gear, and lessons from Mir).

Emergency: Presents environment-aware triage for three scenarios (Active Flame, CO / Smoke, and Burn), with response checklists, a containment progress indicator, and a copyable brief.

Space & Earth Safety: Lets users describe a product or polymer (for example polyethylene food packaging, protective clothing, cable insulation, or an industrial smoke sensor) and see how knowledge from space combustion research can inform safer material selection and fire prevention on Earth, accessible beyond specialists.

From a technical perspective, AstroPyre Intelligence was developed as a self-contained single-page web application (index.html) using HTML5, CSS, Vanilla JavaScript, and HTML5 Canvas. It is hosted through GitHub Pages and runs entirely on the client side over a curated dataset of NASA sources, without an external backend. The AI Search box in each mode runs local retrieval over this dataset, with no model call. In AI Insights, plain-language briefings and investigation summaries were drafted with Claude from collected NASA sources, each statement carrying its source, and are being verified by our team. An optional "Ask the sources" box calls a live model (Claude) only when the page is opened inside claude.ai, on the viewer's own account and with consent; otherwise it falls back to local retrieval. Gemini and Claude also assisted with interface development, while our team reviewed and refined the results.

Our innovation lies in connecting scientific evidence, interactive visualizations, and historical lessons within a unified, accessible environment. Rather than simply displaying research findings, AstroPyre Intelligence encourages users to actively explore combustion-related phenomena and their safety implications.

Throughout development, we prioritized scientific accuracy, accessibility, intuitive navigation, and a clear distinction between verified experimental findings and simplified heuristic estimates. For example, we state openly that our Flammability Lab starts from 1 g oxygen index values and may underestimate risk in microgravity. We also considered the constraints of spacecraft and habitat environments, astronaut safety, and the transfer of space research insights to applications on Earth.

Our primary goal is to make microgravity combustion research easier to understand and apply, support safer material selection, and strengthen emergency preparedness. In the long term, AstroPyre Intelligence aims to contribute to safer human space exploration, including future habitats such as Mars, while encouraging innovations in fire prevention, safer product design, and risk awareness on Earth.
